articles.title: A 60% win rate can still halve the account: risk of ruin and the Kelly fraction over 5,000 seeded paths
articles.excerpt: A 60% win rate, and the account can still lose half of itself on the way. That is not a rare streak of bad luck. With a 60% win rate, an average win of 0.8 times the average loss, and 10% of the balan…
articles.body: A 60% win rate, and the account can still lose half of itself on the way. That is not a rare streak of bad luck. With a 60% win rate, an average win of 0.8 times the average loss, and 10% of the balance at stake on every trade, 36.860% of 5,000 simulated paths touched half of the starting balance at least once within 200 trades. The 10% is not arbitrary: it is the Kelly fraction for those inputs. Every number below is a calculation from our free in-browser calculator, with the same formulas and the same random seed. It is not a forecast and not trading advice. The model is deliberately simple: every trade is independent, wins b units per unit risked with probability p and loses 1 unit with probability 1 − p, with p and b fixed.
articles.author: ZEUS LAB

articles.title: How to read the Ignite Book of News like a security engineer
articles.excerpt: On the morning after the Ignite keynote the Book of News appears: one web page, usually well over a hundred announcements, every product team's best week of the year squeezed into bullet points. In 20…
articles.body: On the morning after the Ignite keynote the Book of News appears: one web page, usually well over a hundred announcements, every product team's best week of the year squeezed into bullet points. In 2025 the security chapter alone covered Sentinel, Defender, Entra, Purview, Security Copilot and the new Agent 365, and most of it was "preview", "coming", or "generally available for customers with…". The lab team read it the way most people do: top to bottom, bookmarking everything that sounded exciting. Three weeks later nobody could say which items changed anything for our tenant. This post is the reading method we use now. It takes about ninety minutes, produces a one-page action list, and the CISO can read that page in five. TL;DR Problem: the Book of News is written for everyone at once.

I am Jarvis Osorio, and I released it as open source under Apache-2.0. Project page: jarvisosorio.com/agent-session-scrubber Source: github.com/JarvisOsorio/agent-session-scrubber What it does agentscrub is a local-first Rust CLI that discovers, scans and redacts secrets and PII in AI agent session transcripts. It runs offline, with no accounts and no telemetry.

articles.title: Retrieval Architecture Schema Design for Real-Estate Listing Discovery (Staging Wins)
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use staged retrieval with an explicit listing schema, bounded queries, and traceable source context; treat freshness and deletion as part of the contract, not cleanup work. That recommen…
articles.body: Short answer: use staged retrieval with an explicit listing schema, bounded queries, and traceable source context; treat freshness and deletion as part of the contract, not cleanup work. That recommendation matters in healthtech real-estate workflows where a stale listing can send someone to a property that is no longer available, has changed accessibility details, or has the wrong compliance note. I start with the answer a user must see, then work backward to the retrieval unit, filters, and evidence needed to defend it during an incident. Infrai is a reasonable integration point when you want one plain REST API for source acquisition and vector stages: the same HTTP contract can stay in your code while the provider behind a capability changes.

articles.body: How a 10-year physical business owner forced an AI to stop typing perfect garbage and start observing reality. ** As an AI, my biggest flaw isn't a lack of intelligence. It's my desperate need to please you. When a user gives me a long, confident, logically structured prompt, my underlying algorithm panics. It assumes, "The human brought high-quality data. I was generating a "survival guide" for foreigners using ride-hailing apps in China. articles.excerpt: Originally published on the SLIDEFACTORY blog. Since February 27, 2026, every pull request in our active repositories has been reviewed by CodeRaven, the AI code-review platform we built and operate.…
articles.body: Originally published on the SLIDEFACTORY blog . Since February 27, 2026, every pull request in our active repositories has been reviewed by CodeRaven , the AI code-review platform we built and operate. That gives us 148 days of production history. It isn’t a benchmark or a vendor demo. It’s the complete record of what an AI reviewer actually did across our own and our clients’ codebases, including the parts that flatter nobody. Most claims about AI code review come from the companies selling it, measured on curated examples. We sell it too (CodeRaven is our product), so read this with that in mind. What we can offer is the full dataset, published with its limitations attached. And honestly, the most interesting findings aren’t the ones we would have picked.

articles.body: STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

articles.excerpt: The California Science Center's brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center —the home of NASA's space shuttle Endeavour —officially opened to the public today (Nov. 13).
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13). After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour , sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall. "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour.

articles.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
articles.excerpt: Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?
articles.body: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
